section_1.title: Introduction: The Chaos and Order of Primes
section_1.content: A 60-second visual hook: Visualize the distribution of prime numbers on a number line compared to a random noise distribution. Introduce the 'Prime Number Theorem' as the heartbeat of mathematical regularity.
section_1.example: Visualize prime numbers as 'fireflies' blinking in a vast dark forest of integers, appearing chaotic but following a specific statistical density.

section_2.title: Prime Patterns & Pi: The Basel Connection
section_2.content: Transition from prime distribution to the Riemann Zeta function. Explain that the probability of two random integers being coprime is 6/π². Show how the infinite product formula bridges the gap between discrete primes and the circular constant π.
section_2.example: Imagine a 'Raindrop Experiment': If you drop pins randomly on a grid, the ratio of coprime pairs eventually settles toward a value dictated by π.

section_3.title: Dirichlet’s Theorem: The Prime Highway
section_3.content: Define Dirichlet’s Theorem on arithmetic progressions. Explain that for any two coprime integers a and d, there are infinitely many primes of the form a + nd. Emphasize this as the bridge between modular arithmetic and infinite prime distributions.
section_3.example: Use a 'Multi-lane Highway' analogy: If the starting point and lane width (a and d) share no common factors, every lane will eventually be crowded with infinite prime 'cars'.

section_4.title: Synthesis & Visual Summary
section_4.content: Combine the concepts: Prime distribution governs the Zeta function, which yields π, while Dirichlet ensures these primes populate every 'lane' of modular arithmetic. A 60-second animated summary showing these threads weaving together.
section_4.example: A 'Loom' animation where threads labeled 'Primes', 'Pi', and 'Modular Arithmetic' are woven into a single, cohesive tapestry representing the fabric of number theory.
